title: How Whiteboard Walkthrough Works
subtitle: A Claude Code plugin that turns a design, proposal or decision into a narrated whiteboard page like this one. This page was built by the plugin itself.

steps.title: The whole picture
steps.say: This page was made by the plugin it describes, so you're watching the thing explain itself. The board has four bands, one for each place something happens: online at the top, then Claude Code, then your computer, and at the bottom, where people watch. Time runs left to right: installing once, each time you ask, the build, then sharing. Green boxes are what the plugin adds, plain outlines are things you already have, red dashed lines are the failure path, and grey dotted lines are the catch-all.

steps.title: Installing once
steps.say: Start at the top left, the green box online: the plugin repo. It holds one skill and three small scripts, the builder, the voices and the page player, plus a worked example to copy. You add its marketplace and install the plugin once, with two commands in Claude Code. That's the line down to the second green box. After that, every project you open has the skill, and updates arrive when the repo changes.

steps.title: Asking for a walkthrough
steps.say: Follow the line right. Whenever you have a design, a proposal or a decision to explain, you ask for a walkthrough, in plain words or with the slash command. Claude loads the skill file, the next green box. It holds the craft: how to draw the board, and how to talk someone through it. It also says where its scripts live, so it works from whatever folder you're in, and you never have to run the scripts yourself.

steps.title: The drawing rules
steps.say: First, the drawing rules. Bands are for where things run, and columns are for when, left to right. Every box is marked new, existing, changed or failure; in your own walkthroughs, an amber dashed box marks a part your design changes. The failure path and the catch-all have to be drawn, not just the happy path, because that's where the real questions are. And every line lists its corner points, so it goes around boxes instead of through them.

steps.title: The speech rules and the spec
steps.say: Then the speech rules. Eight to twelve steps, each sixty to a hundred and ten words. Spoken words only, no symbols, with file names said the way a person would say them. Step one is the whole picture; then the eye moves box by box, happy path first, then the failure path, then the catch-all. The last step is the cost and the decision, with a recommendation. Claude writes all of it into one spec file, in a walkthroughs folder in your project.

steps.title: The builder checks the spec
steps.say: The line drops into your computer, to the builder. It checks the spec before anything else. A broken spec, say a line pointing at a box that doesn't exist, follows the red dashed line left into the red box: the build stops, and Claude fixes the spec and runs it again. Smaller problems are warnings rather than stops: a line that runs through a box, a line whose end misses its box, or a step too long to listen to comfortably.

steps.title: The voice chooser
steps.say: Next, the voice chooser. It tries three voices in order. ElevenLabs, only when you've set a key and told the build it's fine to send the text off your machine. Otherwise the Mac's built in voice, free and private. Otherwise nothing at build time, and the viewer's browser speaks each step. With ElevenLabs, the builder reuses any clip whose text hasn't changed, so an edit only pays for the steps it touched, and it clears each clip's text from your ElevenLabs history.

steps.title: When ElevenLabs says no
steps.say: Now the failure path for the voice, the red dashed line coming back down from ElevenLabs. If the key is wrong, or the balance is too low for the text, the chooser doesn't stop the build. It says so, and falls back to the Mac voice or the browser's. If you asked for ElevenLabs by name, it stops instead, because a quiet switch would be a surprise. Either way, nothing leaves your machine without your say so, and you still get a page that plays.

steps.title: The page, shared
steps.say: The chooser hands on to the page and its audio folder, one clip per step. From there the line drops to where people watch. The page is a static web page with its audio folder beside it: open it from disk, publish it as a Claude artifact if your Claude Code has that tool, or copy both to any web host, the way this one is hosted. Viewers press play, and each step lights up its part of the board while the voice explains it.

steps.title: The catch-all
steps.say: The grey dotted lines are the catch-all, and they meet at the browser voice box. When there's no key and no Mac, the chooser sends every step there, and the page reads each one aloud with the browser's own voice, sentence by sentence. And if a recorded clip fails to load while someone is watching, the page switches that one step to the browser voice instead of going quiet. With no voice at all, the text is still on screen to read along.

steps.title: Cost and the decision
steps.say: The cost. With the Mac or browser voice, nothing: no account, no key, and no text leaves your machine. With ElevenLabs, a five minute walkthrough takes about a thousand credits, a few cents on a paid plan, and only the steps you edit are paid for again. The decision is which voice to start with. I recommend the free voice while you're drafting, and ElevenLabs for the final cut of anything you'll share widely, like this one. To try it, install the plugin and ask for a walkthrough of your next design.
